pos: n. (the “grieving” secession of 1886, led by Abraham Kuyper, from the Netherlands Reformed Church)
etymology: Dutch, from Latin dolere, to grieve; the seceding churches called themselves dolerende, grieving, to say they left in sorrow and not in schism.
biblical_def: The Doleantie was the second great secession from the Netherlands Reformed Church, fifty-two years after the Afscheiding. The crisis came in Amsterdam, where Abraham Kuyper and a confessional majority on the consistory refused to admit to membership young people who had been catechized by liberal ministers and would not confess the faith of the church. The higher boards, under the regulations of 1816, overruled the consistory and claimed control of the congregation's property. In January 1886 the consistory secured the church offices of the Nieuwe Kerk against the boards' men, who forced their way in by sawing through a door panel, and Kuyper with some eighty elders and deacons was suspended and then deposed. Rather than accept the deposition, the consistory and many congregations across the country declared themselves free of the synodical board and took the name of the Netherlands Reformed Churches, grieving. Some two hundred congregations followed. In 1892 most of them united with the churches of the 1834 Secession to form the Reformed Churches in the Netherlands. The Doleantie insisted that the church is governed by Christ through its own officers, not by boards appointed under a royal regulation, and that “upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18) is a promise to the church Christ governs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a consistory as the court of a church, and dolor as pain or grief.
webster_full: CONSIS'TORY, n. A place of justice or the court itself; the court of every diocesan bishop; in the reformed churches, an assembly of ministers and elders.
DO'LOR, n. Pain; grief; distress; anguish; lamentation.
DEPOSI'TION, n. The act of dethroning a king, or the degrading of a person from an office or station.
scriptures: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
Rev 3:11
Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints?
corruption_summary: Consistories deposed for refusing to admit unbelievers to the Lord's Table.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the corruption the Doleantie resisted as the subjection of Christ's church to administrative boards. A consistory was deposed not for heresy or immorality but for refusing to receive members who denied the confession; the boards that deposed it held their authority from a royal regulation, not from Christ. When a church's government will not let its elders keep the table, the word of the risen Christ to Philadelphia applies: “hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown” (Rev 3:11).

The honest caveat is that the property struggle that followed, with lawsuits pressed for decades, sat uneasily with 1Co 6:1, “Dare any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust” (1Co 6:1). The principle to recover is the one the name itself confesses: those who leave an apostate institution should leave grieving, not triumphing.
roots_summary: Greek ekklesia (G1577), church; oikodomeo (G3618), to build; krateo (G2902), to hold fast.
roots_lines: Greek ekklesia (G1577) — the called-out assembly, church; Matthew 16:18.
Greek krateo (G2902) — to hold fast, seize; Revelation 3:11.
Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, go to law; 1 Corinthians 6:1.
usage: “upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18) — Christ, not the board, as builder.
“hold that fast which thou hast” (Rev 3:11) — the consistory's charge.
“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the ground of the grieving churches.

pos: n. (Guillaume Groen van Prinsterer, 1801–1876, Dutch historian and statesman, author of Unbelief and Revolution)
etymology: Dutch groen, green; van Prinsterer, a family name of uncertain origin.
biblical_def: Guillaume Groen van Prinsterer was a Leiden-trained jurist and historian, a pupil of Bilderdijk, and for many years archivist of the House of Orange, whose correspondence he edited in many volumes. Converted through the Reveil in the 1820s and 1830s, he became the first great Christian statesman of the modern Netherlands. In 1845–46 he gave a series of private lectures, published in 1847 as Unbelief and Revolution, arguing that the French Revolution was the logical outworking of a theory that sets man's sovereignty in the place of God's, and that every concession to its principle leads further from Christ. His watchword was against the Revolution, the Gospel. In parliament he defended the persecuted Seceders' liberty of worship though he was not one of them, and he spent decades in the school struggle, contending that Christian parents had the right to Christian schools. He often stood alone, and coined the phrase in our isolation lies our strength. Kuyper called him his father in the faith and built the Anti-Revolutionary Party on his foundation. His conviction is the proverb's: “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines infidelity as unbelief, the disbelief of the inspiration of the Scriptures, and revolution as an entire change in the constitution of government.
webster_full: INFIDEL'ITY, n. In general, want of faith or belief; a withholding of credit. Disbelief of the inspiration of the Scriptures, or the divine origin of christianity; unbelief.
REVOLU'TION, n. In politics, a material or entire change in the constitution of government.
STATES'MAN, n. A man versed in the arts of government; usually, one eminent for political abilities.
scriptures: Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people.
Psa 2:12
Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him.
For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us.
Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
corruption_summary: The historian who traced the Revolution to unbelief and answered it with the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the corruption Groen analysed as the doctrine of popular sovereignty, the conviction that authority rises from below and that law is whatever the people will. Scripture locates authority above: “the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king” (Isa 33:22). Groen's point was that this is not a political preference but a theological claim, and that a nation which denies it has already chosen another god.

The modern tendency to read him as a conservative nationalist misses his centre, which was Christ. The command of Psa 2:12 is addressed to rulers, “Kiss the Son, lest he be angry” (Psa 2:12), and Groen believed it. His willingness to defend the Seceders, whose separatism he did not share, is a further lesson: liberty of worship for the faithful is a duty of the Christian magistrate, not a favour.
roots_lines: Hebrew ruwm (H7311) — to exalt, lift up; Proverbs 14:34.
Hebrew nashaq (H5401) — to kiss, do homage; Psalm 2:12.
usage: “Righteousness exalteth a nation” (Pro 14:34) — his politics in a proverb.
“the LORD is our lawgiver” (Isa 33:22) — sovereignty from above.
“Kiss the Son” (Psa 2:12) — the gospel against the Revolution.

pos: n. (Nicolaas Beets, 1814–1903, Dutch preacher, poet, and author of the Camera Obscura under the name Hildebrand)
etymology: Greek Nikolaos, victory of the people; Dutch Beets, a family name.
biblical_def: Nicolaas Beets was the most beloved Dutch author of the nineteenth century. As a Leiden student he published, under the pen-name Hildebrand, the Camera Obscura of 1839, a book of gently humorous sketches of Dutch middle-class life that every Dutch schoolchild came to know. Touched by the Reveil, he gave up a romantic, Byronic manner for evangelical faith, entered the ministry, and served as pastor at Heemstede and Utrecht, becoming one of the most sought-after preachers in the country; from 1874 to 1884 he was professor of church history at Utrecht. Beets belonged to the irenical, ethical wing of the national church: warmly evangelical in his preaching of sin and grace, devoted to Scripture and to prayer, but unwilling to press confessional discipline or to follow either the Seceders of 1834 or Kuyper's Doleantie out of the church. He wrote hymns and devotional verse as well as sermons and essays, and his piety was genuine and tender. He is an example of the preacher who “sought to find out acceptable words” (Ecc 12:10), and of the power of “a word spoken in due season” (Pro 15:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a preacher as one who discourses publicly on religious subjects.
webster_full: PREACH'ER, n. One who discourses publicly on religious subjects; one that is licensed or authorized to preach the gospel.
IREN'ICAL, a. Peaceful; desiring or promoting peace.
SKETCH, n. An outline or general delineation of any thing; a first rough or incomplete draught of a plan.
scriptures: The preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth.
A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it!
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
corruption_summary: A genuinely evangelical preacher whose irenicism left the national church's unbelief undisciplined.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Beets' preaching was sound in its centre, and his writing is a gift to Dutch letters. The temptation his career represents is the gentle one: a piety so warm and so averse to conflict that it will preach Christ beside men who deny Him and never ask the church to choose. Paul joins the preaching and the reproof in one charge: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort” (2Ti 4:2).

The principle to recover is that peace in the church is the fruit of truth, not a substitute for it. The ethical theologians' refusal of discipline left the pulpits Beets loved open to the modernists whom the Seceders and the Doleantie would not tolerate.
roots_summary: Hebrew chephets (H2656), delight, acceptable; dabar (H1697), word; Greek kerusso (G2784), to preach.
usage: “acceptable words” (Ecc 12:10) — the preacher as craftsman.
“a word spoken in due season, how good is it!” (Pro 15:23) — the gift of Hildebrand.
“reprove, rebuke, exhort” (2Ti 4:2) — the half of the charge irenicism forgets.

pos: n. (the Vrije Universiteit, founded in Amsterdam by Abraham Kuyper in 1880, free of both state and church)
etymology: Dutch vrij, free; Latin universitas, the whole, a corporation of masters and scholars.
biblical_def: The Free University of Amsterdam was opened on 20 October 1880 by Abraham Kuyper and a society of Reformed supporters who believed that the state universities had become schools of unbelief. It was free in two directions: free from the state, which neither funded nor governed it, and free from the church, because Kuyper held that learning is its own sphere under Christ and should be governed by those called to it, not by synods. Its charter bound it to the Reformed principles of the Three Forms of Unity. At the opening Kuyper delivered his address on sphere sovereignty, in which he spoke the famous sentence that there is not a square inch in the whole domain of human existence over which Christ, who is sovereign over all, does not cry, Mine. The university began with a handful of professors and students and grew into a major institution; Herman Bavinck taught there from 1902, and it trained generations of Reformed ministers, jurists, and scholars. In the twentieth century it drifted from its foundation and is now a secular university. Its founding text was Paul's: “all things were created by him, and for him” (Col 1:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a university as an assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences.
webster_full: UNIVERS'ITY, n. An assemblage of colleges established in any place, with professors for instructing students in the sciences and other branches of learning.
FREE, a. Being at liberty; not being under necessity or restraint, physical or moral.
CHAR'TER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man.
scriptures: Col 1:16

For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:
Pro 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever.
corruption_summary: A Reformed university founded on the lordship of Christ over learning, and later lost to it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The conviction behind the Free University is the one modern academia denies most fiercely: that there is no neutral learning, and that “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10) is a claim about knowledge, not only about piety. Kuyper's programme was Paul's, “bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ” (2Co 10:5).

The second lesson is the university's own history. An institution freed from the church's oversight in the name of sphere sovereignty proved unable to keep its confession once its professors ceased to hold it. The principle to recover is that freedom from the state is not sufficient; a Christian school must also be bound, in practice and not only on paper, to the faith it was founded to serve.
roots_summary: Greek ktizo (G2936), to create; Hebrew yirah (H3374), fear; chokmah (H2451), wisdom.
usage: “all things were created by him, and for him” (Col 1:16) — the claim of 1880.
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10) — the first principle of learning.
“every thought to the obedience of Christ” (2Co 10:5) — the scholar's calling.

pos: n. (the Dutch Christian political party founded by Abraham Kuyper in 1879 on the principles of Groen van Prinsterer)
etymology: Greek anti, against; Latin revolutio, a turning back, overthrow.
biblical_def: The Anti-Revolutionary Party was founded on 3 April 1879 by Abraham Kuyper as the first modern political party in the Netherlands, with a national organization, a written programme, and local electoral clubs. Its name came from Groen van Prinsterer's analysis: the party existed to oppose not change as such, but the principle of the French Revolution, that sovereignty belongs to the people apart from God. Its programme confessed that the authority of government rests on God's ordinance, that the state is bound by the eternal principles of God's Word though it may not coerce the conscience, and that the family, the church, the school, and the other spheres of life have their own God-given authority which the state must respect. Its first great cause was the school struggle, the demand that Christian schools receive equal public funding with state schools, won in 1917. In alliance with the Roman Catholic party it formed governments from 1888, and Kuyper himself was prime minister from 1901 to 1905. The party merged into a broader Christian Democratic party in 1980. Its foundation was Paul's: “there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a party as a number of persons united in opinion, in opposition to others in the community.
webster_full: PAR'TY, n. A number of persons united in opinion or design, in opposition to others in the community.
SOV'EREIGNTY, n. Supreme power; supremacy; the possession of the highest power, or of uncontrollable power.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
Isa 9:6

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.
For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
corruption_summary: Christian politics organized against the sovereignty of the people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The ARP is a case study in the possibilities and the costs of Christian political organization. Its conviction was right: civil authority is a ministry of God, and the government is ultimately upon the shoulder of the Son, of whose kingdom Isa 9:6 says “the government shall be upon his shoulder” (Isa 9:6). Its achievement in the school struggle secured for Christian parents a liberty most Western nations still deny them.

Its cost was coalition. A party that governs by alliance with Rome must keep silent about what divides it from Rome, and a party that merges into a broad Christian Democratic movement soon has no confession left to keep. The principle to recover is Christ's distinction, “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21): the church must not become a party, and a Christian party must not forget that it answers to God.
roots_summary: Greek exousia (G1849), authority; tasso (G5021), to ordain; Hebrew misrah (H4951), government.
roots_lines: Greek apodidomi (G591) — to render, give back; Matthew 22:21.
usage: “the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) — authority from above.
“the government shall be upon his shoulder” (Isa 9:6) — Christ's kingship over the state.
“a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2) — the end of civil order.

pos: n. (the Christian Reformed Church in North America, formed in 1857 by Dutch Seceder congregations in Michigan)
etymology: From the Dutch Christelijke Gereformeerde Kerk, the name of the Seceder churches in the Netherlands.
biblical_def: The Christian Reformed Church began in April 1857 when four congregations of Dutch immigrants in western Michigan withdrew from the Classis of Holland, which had joined the Reformed Church in America in 1850. The seceders objected that the eastern church sang hymns rather than psalms, admitted to the Lord's Table without careful supervision, neglected catechism preaching, and tolerated Freemasons among its members; they wished to be the American branch of the Seceder churches their fathers had founded in 1834. The church grew slowly until the 1880s, when the RCA's refusal to discipline Masonic membership and a great wave of new immigrants brought it rapid increase. It founded a Theological School in Grand Rapids in 1876, later Calvin College and Calvin Theological Seminary, and its teachers included Geerhardus Vos and Louis Berkhof. The synod of 1924 adopted three points on common grace and deposed Herman Hoeksema's party. In later generations the church moved toward broad evangelicalism, began opening the offices of minister and elder to women in 1995, and only in 2022 reaffirmed its confession on marriage and sexuality after years of controversy. Its founding conviction was the prophet's question: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a denomination as a class or society of individuals called by the same name, as a sect.
webster_full: DENOMINA'TION, n. A class, or society of individuals, called by the same name; as a denomination of christians.
FREEMA'SON, n. One of a society of masons, composed of persons who are united for some social purposes; a fraternity bound by secrecy.
CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
scriptures: Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Eph 4:5
One Lord, one faith, one baptism,
But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.
Rev 3:11
Behold, I come quickly: hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown.
corruption_summary: A Seceder church planted in Michigan in 1857, and its long road from psalms to women in office.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names the CRC's decision, begun in 1995, to open the offices of minister and elder to women as corruption of the apostolic order. Paul's rule is not a cultural accommodation but a creation ordinance: “I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man” (1Ti 2:12), grounded in the verses that follow on Adam's formation first. A church founded to keep the Seceders' strictness gave up a plain apostolic command within four generations.

The pattern is instructive. The 1857 founders were mocked for leaving over hymns and Freemasonry, but they understood that a church loses its confession by small accommodations, each defended as minor. The words of Christ to Philadelphia remain the charge: “hold that fast which thou hast” (Rev 3:11). The 2022 reaffirmation on marriage shows that a confessional remnant can still be heard in a denomination that has drifted.
roots_summary: Hebrew yaad (H3259), to agree, meet by appointment; Greek authenteo (G831), to usurp authority.
roots_lines: Hebrew yaad (H3259) — to meet by appointment, agree; Amos 3:3.
Greek authenteo (G831) — to exercise authority over; 1 Timothy 2:12.
usage: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3) — the question of 1857.
“One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph 4:5) — unity on a confession.
“nor to usurp authority over the man” (1Ti 2:12) — the command set aside in 1995.

pos: n. (Foppe Martin ten Hoor, 1855–1934, Seceder-trained minister and professor of dogmatics at the Christian Reformed seminary in Grand Rapids)
etymology: Frisian Foppe, a personal name; Dutch ten Hoor, at the Hoor, a place-name.
biblical_def: Foppe ten Hoor was trained at Kampen in the tradition of the 1834 Secession, served congregations in the Netherlands, and came to America to serve the Christian Reformed Church. In 1900 he was appointed professor of systematic theology at the church's Theological School in Grand Rapids, and he taught there for over two decades. Ten Hoor is remembered as the leading American spokesman for the Seceder understanding of the church against the views associated with Abraham Kuyper. Where Kuyper's followers spoke of the pluriformity of the church and distinguished sharply between the church as institute and as organism, Ten Hoor insisted that the visible, instituted church with its offices, sacraments, and discipline is the church Christ founded, and that the Reformed confession of the marks of the true church in the Belgic Confession must not be softened into a theory of many legitimate forms. He also resisted Kuyper's doctrine of presumptive regeneration. His was a sober, churchly theology that prized the confession above speculation. His conviction rested on the apostle's plea for “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3), and on the body that holds the Head, “knit together” (Col 2:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dogmatics as relating to doctrine, and the church as the collective body of Christians.
webster_full: DOGMAT'IC, a. Pertaining to a dogma, or to settled opinion.
CHURCH, n. The collective body of christians, or of those who profess to believe in Christ, and acknowledge him to be the Savior of mankind.
INSTITU'TION, n. The act of establishing; establishment; that which is appointed, prescribed or founded by authority.
scriptures: Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Col 2:19
And not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God.
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: A Seceder dogmatician who defended the instituted church against pluriformity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error Ten Hoor resisted has grown since his day: a doctrine of the church so spiritualized that every denomination is a legitimate expression of the one church, and none may say that another lacks the marks of a true church. Scripture's body is one body holding one Head, “from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered” (Col 2:19).

The principle to recover is that the church is an institution Christ builds, with offices He appoints, and that the confession's marks of pure preaching, right sacraments, and faithful discipline are tests, not ideals. Paul's charge to Timothy is the dogmatician's: “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).
roots_summary: Greek henotes (G1775), unity; sundesmos (G4886), bond; sumbibazo (G4822), to knit together.
usage: “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3) — unity, not pluriformity.
“not holding the Head” (Col 2:19) — the mark of a false body.
“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — dogmatics as stewardship.

pos: n. (Herman Hoeksema, 1886–1965, Grand Rapids minister deposed after the Christian Reformed synod of 1924 and founder of the Protestant Reformed Churches)
etymology: Dutch Herman, from Germanic heri, army, and man; Frisian Hoeksema, of the corner.
biblical_def: Herman Hoeksema came from Groningen to America as a boy, studied at Calvin Seminary, and became the forceful pastor of the Eastern Avenue Christian Reformed Church in Grand Rapids. With Henry Danhof he attacked the doctrine of common grace developed by Kuyper and Bavinck. In 1924 the CRC synod at Kalamazoo adopted three points: that God shows a favourable attitude toward all men, including in the general offer of the gospel; that God restrains sin in the unregenerate; and that the unregenerate can perform civil good. Hoeksema rejected all three as contrary to the Reformed doctrine of particular grace. His classis suspended and deposed him and his consistory in 1924 and 1925, and with Danhof and George Ophoff he formed the Protestant Reformed Churches. He developed a theology of the covenant as a bond of friendship between God and His elect alone, denied that God in any sense desires the salvation of the reprobate, and wrote a large Reformed Dogmatics. His zeal for sovereign grace was real; but Scripture testifies that God “maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good” (Mat 5:45), and that He says, “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Eze 33:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grace as the free unmerited love and favor of God.
webster_full: GRACE, n. Favorable influence of God; divine influence or the influence of the spirit, in renewing the heart and restraining from sin. The free unmerited love and favor of God.
DEPOSI'TION, n. The act of degrading of a person from an office or station.
COV'ENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing.
scriptures: Mat 5:45
That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.

Say unto them, As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel?
Nevertheless he left not himself without witness, in that he did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.
The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.
corruption_summary: A champion of particular grace who denied God's goodness to the reprobate and the free offer of the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: The dictionary names Hoeksema's denial of the free offer as an error, while honouring his intent. Particular grace and the sincere call of the gospel to all men are both scriptural, and a system that keeps the first by denying the second has let logic overrule the text. Christ wept over Jerusalem, “how often would I have gathered thy children together” (Mat 23:37), and the Lord says by Ezekiel, “turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die” (Eze 33:11).

His opponents were not blameless; the speed with which the classes moved from a synodical declaration to depositions left a lasting wound. The principle to recover is that the goodness of God to all His creatures is confessed in Scripture itself: “The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works” (Psa 145:9). That is not saving grace; it is not nothing.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaphets (H2654), to delight in; tob (H2896), good; Greek agathopoieo (G15), to do good.
roots_lines: Greek anatello (G393) — to cause to rise; Matthew 5:45.
Hebrew chaphets (H2654) — to delight in, have pleasure; Ezekiel 33:11.
usage: “sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust” (Mat 5:45) — the first point of 1924.
“he left not himself without witness” (Act 14:17) — goodness among the nations.
“I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Eze 33:11) — the text he could not reconcile.

pos: n. (the agreement of 1801 between the Presbyterian General Assembly and the Congregationalists of Connecticut for joint frontier churches, abrogated in 1837)
etymology: Latin planum, a flat surface, a scheme; unio, oneness.
biblical_def: The Plan of Union was adopted in 1801 by the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church and the General Association of Connecticut to avoid competition on the New York and Ohio frontier. It allowed Presbyterian and Congregational settlers to form a single congregation, call a minister of either body, and settle disputes either by presbytery or by a council of the congregation, and it allowed committee-men who were not ordained elders to sit in presbyteries. For a generation it planted many churches in the Western Reserve and upstate New York. It also carried New England's theology into the Presbyterian Church: the New Divinity and then the New Haven theology of Nathaniel Taylor, with its denial of imputed sin and its doctrine of man's natural ability, and the revivalism of Charles Finney, who was licensed and ordained by a Plan of Union presbytery. Old School Presbyterians came to see the Plan as the channel of doctrinal corruption and irregular government, and at the General Assembly of 1837 they voted it unconstitutional and exscinded the four synods of Western Reserve, Utica, Geneva, and Genesee that had been formed under it. The Old School and New School then divided until 1869. Its lesson is the apostle's: “A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump” (Gal 5:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a presbytery as a body of elders, and congregationalism as the system in which each congregation is independent.
webster_full: PRES'BYTERY, n. A body of elders in the christian church; in the Presbyterian church, a judicatory consisting of all the ministers within a certain district, and one ruling elder from each parish.
CONGREGA'TIONALIST, n. One who belongs to a congregational church or society; one who holds to the independence of each congregation.
UN'ION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one; concord; agreement and conjunction of mind.
scriptures: Gal 5:9
A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump.
Amo 3:3
Can two walk together, except they be agreed?
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
Jud 17:6
In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
corruption_summary: A frontier convenience that became the channel of New England error into American Presbyterianism.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Plan of Union is the classic case of a union entered for practical advantage before doctrinal and governmental agreement was secured. It was well meant: scattered settlers needed churches, and the two bodies held the same confession on paper. But the prophet's question is not satisfied by paper: “Can two walk together, except they be agreed?” (Amo 3:3).

The principle to recover is that church government is a guardian of doctrine. Presbyteries whose members were not elders and congregations that could choose which polity applied soon could not discipline a minister who denied original sin. The frontier condition Judges describes, when “every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (Jud 17:6), was not cured by blurring the church's order.
roots_summary: Greek zume (G2219), leaven; phurama (G5445), lump; heterozugeo (G2086), to be unequally yoked.
roots_lines: Greek phurama (G5445) — a lump, mass of dough; Galatians 5:9.
Hebrew yaad (H3259) — to agree, meet by appointment; Amos 3:3.
Greek heterozugeo (G2086) — to be unequally yoked; 2 Corinthians 6:14.
usage: “A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump” (Gal 5:9) — the Old School's verdict.
“Can two walk together” (Amo 3:3) — union without agreement.
“right in his own eyes” (Jud 17:6) — frontier order without government.

pos: n. (the doctrinal statement of the New School Presbyterian convention at Auburn, New York, in August 1837)
etymology: Auburn, a town in central New York; Latin declaratio, a making clear.
biblical_def: The Auburn Declaration was adopted by a convention of New School Presbyterians at Auburn, New York, in August 1837, three months after the Old School majority at the General Assembly had abrogated the Plan of Union and exscinded four synods. The Assembly had also issued a testimony listing sixteen doctrinal errors it believed were current in the New School presbyteries, among them the denial that Adam's sin is imputed to his posterity, the claim that men have plenary natural ability to obey God, the reduction of regeneration to the sinner's own act, and a view of the atonement as a governmental display rather than a satisfaction of justice. The Auburn convention answered each error with a corresponding true doctrine, in language that affirmed original sin, the necessity of the Spirit's work in regeneration, and the substitutionary character of Christ's death. Many Old School men conceded that its statements, taken by themselves, were orthodox. Their objection was that the New School presbyteries did not discipline ministers who taught the errors the Declaration repudiated, and that a sound statement which is not enforced protects the very men it condemns. The doctrine at stake was Rom 5:19: “by one man's disobedience many were made sinners” (Rom 5:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imputation in theology as the charging of sin or righteousness to the account of another.
webster_full: IMPUTA'TION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution. In theology, the charging of the sins of Adam to his posterity, or of the righteousness of Christ to believers.
DECLARA'TION, n. An affirmation; an open expression of facts or opinions; verbal utterance.
CONVEN'TION, n. An assembly of delegates or representatives for consultation on important concerns, civil, political or ecclesiastical.
scriptures: Rom 5:19
For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
Eph 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Jer 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
Psa 51:5
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
corruption_summary: An orthodox-sounding answer to charges of New School error, offered by men who would not discipline it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Auburn Declaration is a reminder that the question in a doctrinal controversy is rarely what a party will sign, but what it will tolerate. The errors the Assembly listed were real, and they ran from Taylor's New Haven theology through the revivalism of the burned-over district: a sinner able of himself, a regeneration he performs, an atonement that satisfies no one. Scripture's diagnosis is the opposite: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked” (Jer 17:9).

The principle to recover is that subscription without discipline is not orthodoxy. A church that confesses that men are “dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1) while it ordains men who preach natural ability has two confessions, and the one it enforces is the one it believes.
roots_summary: Greek parakoe (G3876), disobedience; kathistemi (G2525), to constitute; Hebrew aqob (H6121), deceitful.
roots_lines: Hebrew chuwl (H2342) — to be shapen, brought forth; Psalm 51:5.
usage: “many were made sinners” (Rom 5:19) — imputation confessed.
“dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1) — the answer to natural ability.
“in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psa 51:5) — original sin from the womb.
